claim: Cytoplasmic dynein is a molecular motor responsible for minus-end-directed cargo transport along microtubules.
source: Cytoplasmic dynein is a molecular motor responsible for minus-end-directed cargo transport along microtubules (MTs).
evidence: This is a well-established fact about dynein stated in the abstract.

claim: Dynein motility has previously been studied on surface-immobilized MTs in vitro, which constrains the motors to move in two dimensions.
source: Dynein motility has previously been studied on surface-immobilized MTs in vitro, which constrains the motors to move in two dimensions.
evidence: This statement references prior experimental approaches and their limitations.

claim: Dynein moves in a helical trajectory around the MT.
source: We found that dynein moves in a helical trajectory around the MT, demonstrating that it generates torque during cargo transport.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Dynein generates torque during cargo transport.
source: We found that dynein moves in a helical trajectory around the MT, demonstrating that it generates torque during cargo transport.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed helical trajectory.

claim: Dynein generates torque in either direction, resulting in bidirectional helical motility.
source: Unlike other cytoskeletal motors that produce torque in a specific direction, dynein generates torque in either direction, resulting in bidirectional helical motility.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental observations of both left- and right-handed helical movement.

claim: Dynein has a net preference to move along a right-handed helical path.
source: Dynein has a net preference to move along a right-handed helical path, suggesting that the heads tend to bind to the closest tubulin binding site in the forward direction when taking sideways steps.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of helical movement directionality in the results.

claim: Dynein heads tend to bind to the closest tubulin binding site in the forward direction when taking sideways steps.
source: Dynein has a net preference to move along a right-handed helical path, suggesting that the heads tend to bind to the closest tubulin binding site in the forward direction when taking sideways steps.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation suggested by the authors based on the observed right-handed preference.

claim: Bidirectional helical motility may allow dynein to avoid roadblocks in dense cytoplasmic environments during cargo transport.
source: This bidirectional helical motility may allow dynein to avoid roadblocks in dense cytoplasmic environments during cargo transport.
evidence: This is a speculative functional interpretation of the observed bidirectional helical motility.

claim: Surface-immobilized Tetrahymena axonemal dynein motors rotated MTs about their principal axes while translocating them.
source: Such helical movement was first observed in a filament gliding assay in which surface-immobilized Tetrahymena axonemal dynein motors rotated MTs about their principal axes while translocating them (Vale and Toyoshima, 1988).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Helical movement of cargoes has been demonstrated for several members of the myosin and kinesin superfamilies.
source: Helical movement of cargoes has subsequently been demonstrated for several members of the myosin and kinesin superfamilies (Nishizaka et al., 1993; Nitzsche et al., 2008; Yajima et al., 2008; Bormuth et al., 2012; Brunnbauer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Cytoplasmic dynein is the primary MT minus-end directed motor responsible for diverse cellular processes in cargo transport, nuclear positioning, and cell division.
source: Cytoplasmic dynein is the primary MT minus-end directed motor responsible for diverse cellular processes in cargo transport, nuclear positioning, and cell division (Roberts et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and represents established knowledge.

claim: Key aspects of dynein's mechanism remain unclear, including whether or not the motor can produce torque.
source: Despite its importance, key aspects of dynein's mechanism remain unclear, including whether or not the motor can produce torque.
evidence: This statement characterizes the state of knowledge in the field prior to this study.

claim: Kinesin-1 follows a single protofilament track.
source: In contrast to kinesin-1, which follows a single protofilament track (Ray et al., 1993; Yajima and Cross, 2005), dynein takes frequent sideways steps (Reck-Peterson et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Dynein takes frequent sideways steps.
source: In contrast to kinesin-1, which follows a single protofilament track (Ray et al., 1993; Yajima and Cross, 2005), dynein takes frequent sideways steps (Reck-Peterson et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The full trajectory of dynein motors in three dimensions remains unknown.
source: However, the full trajectory of dynein motors in three dimensions (3D) remains unknown, because the motors are sterically prevented from moving around the circumference of surface-immobilized MTs.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge that motivates the current study.

claim: Motors are sterically prevented from moving around the circumference of surface-immobilized MTs.
source: However, the full trajectory of dynein motors in three dimensions (3D) remains unknown, because the motors are sterically prevented from moving around the circumference of surface-immobilized MTs.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the limitations of surface-based assays.

claim: MT bridges allow unconstrained motion between the protofilaments.
source: To track dynein motility in 3D, we constructed MT 'bridges' (Brunnbauer et al., 2012) (Figure 1A), which allow unconstrained motion between the protofilaments.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach and its advantage.

claim: The bridges were constructed by suspending a fluorescently labeled MT between two large (2 µm diameter) polystyrene beads, immobilized on the surface.
source: The bridges were constructed by suspending a fluorescently labeled MT between two large (2 µm diameter) polystyrene beads, immobilized on the surface.
evidence: This describes the experimental method.

claim: The beads were densely coated with a chimeric protein containing the dynein MT binding domain (MTBD) that stably binds to MTs.
source: These beads were densely coated with a chimeric protein containing the dynein MT binding domain (MTBD) that stably binds to MTs (Gibbons et al., 2005; Carter et al., 2008).
evidence: This describes the experimental method and is supported by citations.

claim: Multiple dynein motors were linked to a 0.5-µm diameter bead.
source: Multiple dynein motors were linked to a 0.5-µm diameter bead (referred to as cargo) and brought in proximity of the MT bridge with an optical trap.
evidence: This describes the experimental method.

claim: The xy position of the cargo was determined by a two-dimensional Gaussian tracking algorithm.
source: The xy position of the cargo was determined by a two-dimensional Gaussian tracking algorithm.
evidence: This describes the data analysis method.

claim: The z position was determined by changes in the intensity of the bead center.
source: The z position was determined by changes in the intensity of the bead center (Figure 1C–D), allowing us to track bead movement in 3D.
evidence: This describes the data analysis method and references supporting figures.

claim: The bead center is expected to be separated by ∼250 nm from the MT.
source: The bead center is expected to be separated by ∼250 nm from the MT.
evidence: This is stated in the figure caption and represents a geometric calculation.

claim: Human kinesin-1 motors follow a single protofilament.
source: We initially tested the robustness of our experimental geometry using human kinesin-1 motors, which follow a single protofilament (Ray et al., 1993; Yajima and Cross, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The handedness of the MTs varies based on the number (11–14) of protofilament tracks.
source: Because the handedness of the MTs varies based on the number (11–14) of protofilament tracks (Hyman et al., 1995), we polymerized tubulin with a non-hydrolyzable GTP analog (GMP-CPP).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: 96% of GMP-CPP MTs is made of 14 protofilaments and has a left-handed supertwist with 6400 ± 1000 nm pitch.
source: 96% of GMP-CPP MTs is made of 14 protofilaments and has a left-handed supertwist with 6400 ± 1000 nm pitch (Hyman et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The average velocity of kinesin-driven beads was 541 ± 23 nm/s.
source: The average velocity of kinesin-driven beads was 541 ± 23 nm/s (mean ± SEM, N = 10), comparable to the speed of single motors (Yildiz et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a measurement from the experiments.

claim: The average velocity of kinesin-driven beads is comparable to the speed of single motors.
source: The average velocity of kinesin-driven beads was 541 ± 23 nm/s (mean ± SEM, N = 10), comparable to the speed of single motors (Yildiz et al., 2008).
evidence: This comparison is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Kinesin-1-coated beads travelled along GMP-CPP MTs with a left-handed helical motion with a pitch of 6500 ± 400 nm.
source: We observed that kinesin-1-coated beads travelled along GMP-CPP MTs with a left-handed helical motion with a pitch of 6500 ± 400 nm (mean ±SEM, N = 6) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Video 1), similar to the helicity of 14 protofilament MTs.
evidence: This is a measurement from the experiments shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: The pitch of kinesin-1 helical motion is similar to the helicity of 14 protofilament MTs.
source: We observed that kinesin-1-coated beads travelled along GMP-CPP MTs with a left-handed helical motion with a pitch of 6500 ± 400 nm (mean ±SEM, N = 6) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Video 1), similar to the helicity of 14 protofilament MTs.
evidence: This is a comparison between measured data and known MT structure.

claim: The results are consistent with the reported values of kinesin-1 movement on GMP-CPP MTs (5700–7900 nm pitch, left-handed) using alternative geometries.
source: The results are also consistent with the reported values of kinesin-1 movement on GMP-CPP MTs (5700–7900 nm pitch, left-handed) using alternative geometries (Nitzsche et al., 2008; Brunnbauer et al., 2012).
evidence: This comparison is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: GST-Dyn331kD is a tail-truncated yeast dynein artificially dimerized with glutathione S-transferase.
source: We used a tail-truncated yeast dynein artificially dimerized with glutathione S-transferase (GST-Dyn331kD), which has similar motile properties to full-length dynein (Reck-Peterson et al., 2006).
evidence: This describes the protein construct used in the study.

claim: GST-Dyn331kD has similar motile properties to full-length dynein.
source: We used a tail-truncated yeast dynein artificially dimerized with glutathione S-transferase (GST-Dyn331kD), which has similar motile properties to full-length dynein (Reck-Peterson et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: At 1 mM ATP, dynein-coated beads moved in helical trajectories with a pitch of 591 ± 32 nm.
source: At 1 mM ATP, dynein-coated beads moved in helical trajectories with a pitch of 591 ± 32 nm (mean ± SEM, 67 rotations, 15 beads, Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This is a primary measurement from the experiments.

claim: Dynein's helical rotation corresponds to a sideways movement to a neighboring protofilament (6 nm) for every six tubulin dimers (48 nm) in the forward direction.
source: This rotation corresponds to a sideways movement to a neighboring protofilament (6 nm) for every six tubulin dimers (48 nm) in the forward direction.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the measured pitch and known MT structure.

claim: Beads coated with cytoplasmic dynein exhibited both left- and right-handed helical movement on MTs.
source: Unlike axonemal dynein and kinesin motors, which primarily rotate along their tracks in only one direction (Vale and Toyoshima, 1988; Brunnbauer et al., 2012), beads coated with cytoplasmic dynein exhibited both left- and right-handed helical movement on MTs (N = 67 rotations, Figure 2A–B, Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2, Videos 2,3).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in figures and videos.

claim: Axonemal dynein and kinesin motors primarily rotate along their tracks in only one direction.
source: Unlike axonemal dynein and kinesin motors, which primarily rotate along their tracks in only one direction (Vale and Toyoshima, 1988; Brunnbauer et al., 2012), beads coated with cytoplasmic dynein exhibited both left- and right-handed helical movement on MTs (N = 67 rotations, Figure 2A–B, Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2, Videos 2,3).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The speeds of left- and right-handed movements along the helical path (79 ± 4.7 nm/s and 89 ± 17 nm/s, mean ± SEM, respectively) were statistically indistinguishable.
source: The speeds of left- and right-handed movements along the helical path (79 ± 4.7 nm/s and 89 ± 17 nm/s, mean ± SEM, respectively) were statistically indistinguishable (t-test, p = 0.28).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Beads occasionally switch direction during a run (4 out of 67 rotations).
source: Bidirectional helical movement was also evident from traces of single beads, which occasionally switch direction during a run (4 out of 67 rotations, Figure 2D).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Reversal of bead motility along the MT axis was never observed.
source: In contrast, reversal of bead motility along the MT axis was never observed.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: The average pitch of the left-handed movement (546 ± 42 nm, SEM, N = 32) was shorter than that of the right-handed movement (749 ± 81 nm, SEM, N = 10).
source: The average pitch of the left-handed movement (546 ± 42 nm, SEM, N = 32) was shorter (t-test, p = 0.01) than that of the right-handed movement (749 ± 81 nm, SEM, N = 10).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Full-length yeast cytoplasmic dynein exhibits helical motility with a pitch of 500 ± 36 nm.
source: Dynein-coated beads moved in helical trajectories with a pitch of 500 ± 36 nm (mean ± SEM, Figure 2—figure supplement 3, Video 4) and exhibited both left- and right-handed helical movement.
evidence: This is a measurement from experiments with full-length dynein.

claim: Full-length dynein exhibits both left- and right-handed helical movement.
source: Dynein-coated beads moved in helical trajectories with a pitch of 500 ± 36 nm (mean ± SEM, Figure 2—figure supplement 3, Video 4) and exhibited both left- and right-handed helical movement.
evidence: This is an observation from experiments with full-length dynein.

claim: The velocities of left- and right-handed movement along the helical path for full-length dynein (42 ± 11 nm/s and 43 ± 10 nm/s, mean ± SEM, respectively) were statistically indistinguishable.
source: The velocities of left- and right-handed movement along the helical path (42 ± 11 nm/s and 43 ± 10 nm/s, mean ± SEM, respectively) were statistically indistinguishable (t-test, p = 0.21).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of experimental data for full-length dynein.

claim: Beads driven by full-length dynein occasionally switch direction during a run (8 out of 33 rotations).
source: Similar to GST-Dyn331kD, beads driven by full-length dynein occasionally switch direction during a run (8 out of 33 rotations, Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is an observation from experiments with full-length dynein.

claim: GST-Dyn331kD has a net preference for left-handed helical movement (75%).
source: Unlike GST-Dyn331kD, which has a net preference for left-handed helical movement (75%), full-length dynein has a net preference for right-handed helical movement (58%, t-test, p = 10−5).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Full-length dynein has a net preference for right-handed helical movement (58%).
source: Unlike GST-Dyn331kD, which has a net preference for left-handed helical movement (75%), full-length dynein has a net preference for right-handed helical movement (58%, t-test, p = 10−5).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The difference in handedness preference between GST-Dyn331kD and full-length dynein may be related to GST dimerization, in which the heads may be oriented differently relative to the MT surface.
source: This difference may be related to GST dimerization, in which the heads may be oriented differently relative to the MT surface.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed difference.

claim: The pitch of dynein-driven rotation is much shorter than the supertwist of the GMP-CPP MTs (∼6400 nm).
source: The pitch of dynein-driven rotation is much shorter than the supertwist of the GMP-CPP MTs (∼6400 nm), suggesting that helical motility of dynein is independent from the helicity of the MT track.
evidence: This is a comparison between measured data and known MT structure.

claim: Helical motility of dynein is independent from the helicity of the MT track.
source: The pitch of dynein-driven rotation is much shorter than the supertwist of the GMP-CPP MTs (∼6400 nm), suggesting that helical motility of dynein is independent from the helicity of the MT track.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of dynein's pitch with MT supertwist.

claim: Taxol-stabilized MTs contain a mixture of 12 (77%) and 13 (11%) and 14 (2%) protofilaments.
source: To verify this, we repeated the assay with GST-Dyn331kD on taxol-stabilized MTs, which contain a mixture of 12 (77%) and 13 (11%) and 14 (2%) protofilaments (Ray et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Out of 34 rotations on taxol-stabilized MTs, 68% were left-handed and 32% were right-handed.
source: Out of 34 rotations, 68% were left-handed and 32% were right-handed.
evidence: This is a measurement from experiments on taxol-stabilized MTs.

claim: On taxol-stabilized MTs, the average pitch of helical movement was 607 ± 50 nm.
source: On average, the pitch of helical movement was 607 ± 50 nm (mean ±SEM) (Figure 2—figure supplement 5), similar to that of GMP-CPP MTs (t-test, p=0.77).
evidence: This is a measurement from experiments on taxol-stabilized MTs.

claim: The pitch of helical movement on taxol-stabilized MTs is similar to that of GMP-CPP MTs.
source: On average, the pitch of helical movement was 607 ± 50 nm (mean ±SEM) (Figure 2—figure supplement 5), similar to that of GMP-CPP MTs (t-test, p=0.77).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of experimental data.

claim: The findings are not an artifact of the MT polymerization method.
source: The results demonstrate that our findings are not an artifact of the MT polymerization method.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the similarity of results between GMP-CPP and taxol-stabilized MTs.

claim: The average run length of single GST-Dyn331kD motors on MT bridges was 1.5 ± 0.2 µm.
source: The average run length of single motors on MT bridges was 1.5 ± 0.2 µm (mean ± SEM, N = 10), which is similar to that measured on surface-immobilized MTs (Reck-Peterson et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a measurement from single-motor experiments.

claim: The run length of single motors on MT bridges is similar to that measured on surface-immobilized MTs.
source: The average run length of single motors on MT bridges was 1.5 ± 0.2 µm (mean ± SEM, N = 10), which is similar to that measured on surface-immobilized MTs (Reck-Peterson et al., 2006).
evidence: This comparison is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The velocity of single GST-Dyn331kD dimers was 64 ± 8 nm/s.
source: The velocity of single dimers was 64 ± 8 nm/s (mean ± SEM, N = 10), similar (t-test, p = 0.12) to that of cargo beads carried by multiple dimers (80 ± 10 nm/s, N = 15).
evidence: This is a measurement from single-motor experiments.

claim: The velocity of single dimers is similar to that of cargo beads carried by multiple dimers.
source: The velocity of single dimers was 64 ± 8 nm/s (mean ± SEM, N = 10), similar (t-test, p = 0.12) to that of cargo beads carried by multiple dimers (80 ± 10 nm/s, N = 15).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of experimental data.

claim: The traces of single motors show high variability along the perpendicular axis of MTs.
source: The traces of single motors show high variability along the perpendicular axis of MTs and switch directions in their sideways movement more frequently than the beads carried by multiple motors (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is an observation from single-motor tracking experiments.

claim: Single motors switch directions in their sideways movement more frequently than the beads carried by multiple motors.
source: The traces of single motors show high variability along the perpendicular axis of MTs and switch directions in their sideways movement more frequently than the beads carried by multiple motors (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is an observation from single-motor tracking experiments.

claim: The results exclude rotational tug-of-war.
source: These results exclude rotational tug-of-war.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the observation that single motors do not show regular helical movement.

claim: Monomeric Dyn331kD is not processive on its own.
source: To eliminate the contribution of interhead orientation, we used a cargo bead coated with monomeric Dyn331kD, which is not processive on its own (Reck-Peterson et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Multiple monomers were able to drive processive motility of cargo beads at 61 ± 6 nm/s.
source: We observed that multiple monomers were able to drive processive motility of cargo beads at 61 ± 6 nm/s (mean ± SEM), consistent with the ability of multiple non-processive kinesins or myosins to drive processive motility (Kamei et al., 2005; Furuta et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a measurement from experiments with monomeric dynein.

claim: Multiple non-processive kinesins or myosins can drive processive motility.
source: We observed that multiple monomers were able to drive processive motility of cargo beads at 61 ± 6 nm/s (mean ± SEM), consistent with the ability of multiple non-processive kinesins or myosins to drive processive motility (Kamei et al., 2005; Furuta et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The trajectories of beads driven by dynein monomers displayed a helical component.
source: The trajectories of beads driven by dynein monomers (Figure 4, Video 5) also displayed a helical component.
evidence: This is an observation from experiments with monomeric dynein.

claim: The average pitch for beads driven by monomers was 579 nm ± 38 nm.
source: The average pitch (579 nm ± 38 nm, 57 rotations, 11 beads) was similar to that of GST-Dyn331kD (t-test, p = 0.78) and higher than full-length dynein (t-test, p = 0.16).
evidence: This is a measurement from experiments with monomeric dynein.

claim: The average pitch for beads driven by monomers was similar to that of GST-Dyn331kD.
source: The average pitch (579 nm ± 38 nm, 57 rotations, 11 beads) was similar to that of GST-Dyn331kD (t-test, p = 0.78) and higher than full-length dynein (t-test, p = 0.16).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of experimental data.

claim: The majority (59%) of the rotations for monomers was right-handed.
source: The majority (59%) of the rotations was right-handed, similar to full-length dimers (N-1 two proportion test, p = 0.47).
evidence: This is a measurement from experiments with monomeric dynein.

claim: The handedness preference of monomers is similar to full-length dimers.
source: The majority (59%) of the rotations was right-handed, similar to full-length dimers (N-1 two proportion test, p = 0.47).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of experimental data.

claim: The speeds of left- and right-handed movements along the helical path for monomers (66 ± 10 nm/s and 57 ± 6 nm/s, respectively) were statistically indistinguishable.
source: The speeds of left- and right-handed movements along the helical path (66 ± 10 nm/s and 57 ± 6 nm/s, respectively) were statistically indistinguishable (t-test, p = 0.18).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of experimental data for monomers.

claim: Right-handed preference of full-length dynein for helical movement is not due to the head–head orientation of the dimer.
source: The results indicate that right-handed preference of full-length dynein for helical movement is not due to the head–head orientation of the dimer.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the observation that monomers also show right-handed preference.

claim: Single dynein dimers take frequent sideways steps.
source: In this study, we showed that cytoplasmic dynein moves along MTs in a helical trajectory with a pitch of ∼500 nm. Single dynein dimers take frequent sideways steps (Reck-Peterson et al., 2006), whereas multiple dynein dimers persistently move in a helical path with a net preference for a right-handed rotation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Multiple dynein dimers persistently move in a helical path with a net preference for a right-handed rotation.
source: In this study, we showed that cytoplasmic dynein moves along MTs in a helical trajectory with a pitch of ∼500 nm. Single dynein dimers take frequent sideways steps (Reck-Peterson et al., 2006), whereas multiple dynein dimers persistently move in a helical path with a net preference for a right-handed rotation.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: Kinesin-1 monomers are believed to move to the closest possible site on the microtubule which stays to the left of the previous binding site.
source: Kinesin-1 monomers are believed to move to the closest possible site on the microtubule which stays to the left of the previous binding site (Yajima and Cross, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Kinesin-1 dimers only walk along a single protofilament because their short neck-linker prevents off-axis stepping.
source: However, kinesin-1 dimers only walk along a single protofilament because their short neck-linker prevents off-axis stepping (Brunnbauer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: In dynein, monomers may prefer to attach to the nearest tubulin binding site towards the MT minus end, favoring a rightward step.
source: In dynein, monomers may prefer to attach to the nearest tubulin binding site towards the MT minus end, favoring a rightward step (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a mechanistic model proposed by the authors.

claim: In a dynein dimer, the heads are attached to neighboring protofilaments and the leading head prefers to be on the right side at 30° relative to the trailing head.
source: In the case of a dimer, the heads are attached to neighboring protofilaments and the leading head prefers to be on the right side at 30° relative to the trailing head (DeWitt et al., 2012; Qiu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The orientation of dynein heads would make a rightward step more favorable for the trailing head, resulting in a net rightward bias.
source: This orientation would make a rightward step more favorable for the trailing head, resulting in a net rightward bias (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation based on structural information.

claim: The molecular basis of the switches in helical directionality remains unclear.
source: The molecular basis of the switches in helical directionality remains unclear.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation in understanding the mechanism.

claim: The irregular stepping pattern of individual motors rules out the possibility of a rotational tug-of-war.
source: The irregular stepping pattern of individual motors rules out the possibility of a rotational tug-of-war.
evidence: This conclusion is based on single-motor tracking data.

claim: The helical pattern of bead movement may be determined by the conformations of dynein motors associated with the MT track.
source: Instead, we propose that the helical pattern of bead movement may be determined by the conformations of dynein motors associated with the MT track.
evidence: This is a mechanistic model proposed by the authors.

claim: Dyneins that are bound in sufficiently close proximity to other dyneins experience steric exclusion effects.
source: It is likely that dyneins that are bound in sufficiently close proximity to other dyneins experience steric exclusion effects.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the mechanism.

claim: Individual dynein motors have 1400 nm run length.
source: Individual dynein motors have 1400 nm run length (Reck-Peterson et al., 2006), indicating that motors on the bead detach and reattach during a processive run of a cargo bead.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Motors on the bead detach and reattach during a processive run of a cargo bead.
source: Individual dynein motors have 1400 nm run length (Reck-Peterson et al., 2006), indicating that motors on the bead detach and reattach during a processive run of a cargo bead.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of single motor run length with cargo bead run length.

claim: Changes in motor attachment may alter the orientation of the MT bound motors, resulting in the reversal of helical directionality during a processive run.
source: These may alter the orientation of the MT bound motors, resulting in the reversal of helical directionality during a processive run (Figure 5D), as occasionally observed.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation of the observed directional switches.

claim: Inside cells, the MT surface is crowded with associated proteins, which act as roadblocks during the transport of intracellular cargos.
source: Inside cells, the MT surface is crowded with associated proteins, which act as roadblocks during the transport of intracellular cargos (Stamer et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The intracellular space is crowded with large structures, such as vesicles and organelles.
source: Furthermore, the intracellular space is crowded with large structures, such as vesicles and organelles.
evidence: This is general knowledge about cellular organization.

claim: The ability of molecular motors to produce torque and axial force may allow the motors to switch protofilaments and avoid obstacles.
source: The ability of molecular motors to produce torque and axial force may allow the motors to switch protofilaments and avoid these obstacles.
evidence: This is a speculative functional interpretation.

claim: In cells, the same MT track is used for both plus- and minus-end-directed transport.
source: In cells, the same MT track is used for both plus- and minus-end-directed transport.
evidence: This is general knowledge about cellular transport.

claim: Sideways movement may prevent traffic jams on MTs.
source: Sideways movement may prevent traffic jams on MTs.
evidence: This is a speculative functional interpretation.

claim: Dynein can bypass roadblocks whereas kinesin-1 stalls when it encounters an obstacle and eventually releases.
source: In vitro assays have shown that dynein can bypass roadblocks whereas kinesin-1 stalls when it encounters an obstacle and eventually releases (Dixit et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Bidirectional helical movement may provide additional flexibility to dynein to transport cargos in dense cellular environments.
source: Bidirectional helical movement may provide additional flexibility to dynein to transport cargos in dense cellular environments.
evidence: This is a speculative functional interpretation of the findings.

claim: The bead moves in a left-handed helical manner along the MT.
source: The bead moves in a left-handed helical manner along the MT.
evidence: This describes the observation shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The averaged intensity of a 500 nm diameter bead under brightfield illumination increases as the bead is moved from −250 nm to +250 nm in the z direction relative to the image plane.
source: The averaged intensity from 20 beads increases as the bead is moved from −250 nm to +250 nm in the z direction relative to the image plane.
